title: India's $315 Billion Outsourcing Empire Is Hiring Fewer People. The Firms That Built It Say AI Made the Old Model Obsolete.
excerpt: At the Reuters India Summit, executives from Novo Nordisk, Daimler Truck, Standard Chartered, and Southwest Airlines described a new reality: India remains critical, but the link between growth and hiring has been permanently broken. The Cockroach Janta Party is the internet's answer.
body:
For three decades, the formula was elegant in its simplicity. Western companies needed cheap, skilled labour. India had it in abundance. The outsourcing industry that emerged — from Infosys and Wipro to the global capability centres (GCCs) of every Fortune 500 firm — grew into a $315 billion sector that transformed India's economy, created a massive middle class, and powered the upward mobility of an entire generation of Indian families.

That formula is breaking.

## The Summit That Said the Quiet Part Out Loud

At last week's Reuters India Summit in Mumbai, executive after executive described a world in which India remains central to their global operations — but in which the link between growth and hiring has been severed, possibly permanently.

Novo Nordisk, the Danish pharmaceutical giant, said it was using AI to accelerate drug launches while expanding India's role in global operations. But it expected to be "conservative" on hiring. Daimler Truck said AI tools were helping its Indian engineers "generate IP faster" — and that it was now scouting for "niche talents" in AI and cybersecurity rather than filling seats.

Epsilon, the technology arm of Publicis Groupe, said productivity gains from AI were allowing it to do significantly more work without meaningfully growing headcount. "What has changed is the amount of work that we are delivering, the new responsibilities that we have picked up," said Pratik Nath, Epsilon India's managing director.

The message was consistent across sectors: more output, fewer people, higher skill bars.

## The Numbers Behind the Shift

The anecdotal evidence from the Summit is backed by hard data. Standard Chartered announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs while ramping up AI investment. CEO Bill Winters framed it bluntly: "It's not cost-cutting. It's replacing in some cases lower-value human capital." Many of the affected roles are in the bank's back-office centres in Chennai and Bengaluru — precisely the kinds of jobs that built India's outsourcing reputation.

Lalit Ahuja, CEO of ANSR, which helps multinational firms build and run global centres in India, offered a structural forecast: "Companies are hiring fewer people, just as a matter of abundant caution." Growth and scale from a people standpoint, he said, "will taper over time."

TeamLease Services, one of India's largest staffing firms, reported that companies were being advised to keep 20 to 30 percent of their workforce on outsourced or variable models rather than permanent payrolls. The shift from permanent to contingent hiring is not a recession response — it is a structural adaptation to AI uncertainty.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For millions of Indian Americans and Indian professionals in the UK, Canada, and Australia, the outsourcing industry is not an abstraction. It is the ecosystem that employs their siblings, funds their parents' retirement, and provides the professional pipeline that feeds the H-1B visa system.

If Indian GCCs shift from hiring 1,000 engineers to hiring 300 engineers with AI augmentation, the downstream effects are significant. Fewer entry-level IT jobs in India means fewer candidates with the work experience that typically precedes an H-1B petition. It means fewer campus placements, smaller training cohorts, and a narrower funnel into the global tech workforce.

IBM India head Sandip Patel offered a more optimistic framing: India's demographic dividend could become an AI dividend. "You will be at a 350 million AI-trained workforce that can be deployed not just here, but can be doing work around the world," he said. But the transition from a labour-intensive model to an AI-intensive one is not seamless, and the people in the middle — mid-career IT professionals with domain expertise but no AI fluency — are the most exposed.

## The Cockroach Janta Party

The anxiety is not confined to boardrooms. It has spilled into India's online culture through the rise of the so-called Cockroach Janta Party — an internet movement reflecting frustration over jobs, wages, and economic insecurity among young Indians.

A Deloitte Global survey found that Gen Z respondents in India reported higher financial stress due to job insecurity and rising costs. Many had postponed major life decisions — buying homes, starting families, investing — because they could not see a stable economic path forward.

The Iran war is compounding the problem. Gulf-based jobs that once absorbed surplus Indian labour are drying up as the conflict disrupts regional economies. Remittances from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar — which collectively send tens of billions of dollars to Indian families each year — are under pressure.

## The New Model

Southwest Airlines plans to scale its Hyderabad technology centre to about 1,000 employees. But Krishna Kallepalli, the airline's vice president and global head of innovation for India, was explicit that this was not the old playbook: "We don't want to just do a lift and shift and create another back office. We are looking at business capabilities that are technology-infused."

Kimberly-Clark said employees now needed domain expertise alongside AI literacy. The old skillset — English proficiency, basic coding, process knowledge — is necessary but no longer sufficient. The new bar is higher, the roles are fewer, and the competition is global.

India's outsourcing empire is not collapsing. It is mutating. The $315 billion sector will continue to grow in revenue terms. But the social contract that powered it — bring thousands of young Indians into the middle class through IT jobs — is being rewritten by algorithms that do the same work faster, cheaper, and without health insurance.
nri_angle: India's outsourcing model — which powers H-1B pipelines, campus placements, and the professional mobility of millions of diaspora families — is being fundamentally altered by AI. The shift from headcount-driven growth to AI-augmented productivity means fewer entry-level IT jobs and a narrower funnel into the global tech workforce.
author: Diaspora Desk
